content:
Hi folks, just created this account a few minutes ago, so consider me a genuine lean outsider who's very interested in what's going on here.

I've been working on an autoformalization system whose goal is end-to-end formalization of individual math papers in Lean. In early experiments I was trying really simple frameworks like python scripts that just bounce agents off each other, have one agent direct another, etc., but I encountered both "honesty" and performance (e.g., spinning without real progress) problems. So my system now is much more constrained; it uses LLMs in various roles to certify natural language elaborations of what is being formalized, with "legal next moves" of the autoformalization process controlled by a deterministic finite state machine. The idea is that this approach really gives a way of enforcing real incremental progress.

I plan a write up describing the methodology and a code release shortly. For now I wanted to post because I do have two formalizations up; they are both Ramsey results (these were fun choices for me not just because I liked the papers but because the amount of lean one needs to verify the correct theorem is being proved is so small). The most recent was a a complete end-to-end autoformalization in under 48 hours, using around $18 of chatgpt usage at prorated pro subscription rates; no human input beyond the initial tex file.

The formalizations are linked here:
https://www.math.cmu.edu/~wes/trellis.php

One side effect of how this system works is that in the end, you end with a large set of "nodes" in the lean dependency structure, each with a lean statement and corresponding tex statement, and with with natural language proofs as well as lean proofs connecting all these nodes together. The "formalization viewer" links listed at that site let's you browse that view of each formalization.

Please share any feedback; as I said I am a completely new to the world of lean. I've tried to be careful but am sure at the very least that I am making, e.g., weird stylistic choices that I could improve by hearing from the experts here.

Even though I'm very much a newcomer to Lean myself, I have a few comments/questions.

Generally speaking, I liked very much the documentation. I noticed though that I found myself looking for the context of the formalization: toolchain version, dependencies (including their versions, etc). I may have missed it, but put in simple words, I was looking for the webified TOML. It was easy enough to go to the source code, of course, but I wish I wouldn't have had to. Speaking of which, are dependencies other than Mathlib supported?

Random findings:

  • Another statement that (IMO) would be useful in the documentation: the report on axioms used.
  • Not sure if I'm doing something wrong: I typed "LoopGraph" in the Search nodes field and hit Enter: nothing happened.
  • The "Preamble" node in "Off-Diagonal Ramsey Formalization" is a weird one. No content, is it just common mathlib imports?

You mentioned "code release": any ETA? Also, have you already decided under which licensing terms?

I would also be curious to see the result of an attempt at formalizing a paper which cannot reasonably be 100% formalized (or it could, but you'd have to formalize like five other papers or book chapters first). How does Treillis handle such situations?

Finally, has any thought been given to the question of reusability of the generated code? Or perhaps, simply avoiding to re-implement the same thing during the formalizations of different (but closely related) papers?

Thanks for these suggestions! I've updated the viewers to integrate them.

Yes the preamble node is just for common Mathlib imports. Perhaps I should be presenting that differently.

I would like to release code very soon (within the week) along with a description of the method. This will mostly depend on how much I compromise my standards for what I release ;-) Have not thought about licensing yet but I want mathematicians to be able to use this.

If I gave it a paper that was "too big" in terms of its dependencies, I am confident my systems would prevent incorrect / misleading formalizations but that there would be nothing from stopping it spending a full subscription quota week after week on a task that it would not be well suited to. There is a "NeedInput" escape valve where the process can say it has found an unfixable problem in what it is formalizing but this situation has not happened for me yet and I'm not sure it would likely to be triggered in the situation you're describing.

Currently I don't allow imports other than Mathlib but I am interested in code reusability, for sure. I guess one thing I should be clear on is some things I'm not trying to do right now: I'm not trying to "autoformalize fields of math"; I suspect that generating infrastructure with little human input is easy to do in a way that is not really contributing much. I am also not working on any kind of interaction where humans help or guide the process (other than an acceptance gate where a human is asked to accept the nodes in the semantic closure of nodes covering the paper targets being formalized, before formalization proceeds). One reason I'm not doing that at this stage is that I find it easier to try to be scientific about what makes the system work well when there is no human input involved; even if I want to build an interactive system, I first want to understand how to make the fully automatic system work well. Instead, at this point, I'm think of this system as having the task: here is one paper, formalize the paper, with no human input. I think it is feasible to make this work well enough that Lean becomes much more relevant to a lot of mathematicians today.

The next significant thing I want to implement in the system (not sure if this will be pre- or post-first-release) is a framework for having a specific list of outside dependencies of a paper being formalized that are allowed to be axiomatized (with human approved statements). There are a lot of nice papers it would be reasonable to autoformalize with one or two axiomatized dependencies that are otherwise now not reasonable targets, so I think this would meaningfully improve the utility of the system as a tool to "verify" one paper. Of course, it would make sense to incorporate a system for non-mathlib imports as well. Presumably I will implement that as soon as it comes up for a target I am considering.
I like very much how your viewer for Lean and TeX code looks like!

@Wes Pegden Never compromise with one's own standards and principles. Other than that, thank you for the added details, and I guess we won't wait too long to be able to see and play with your creation.

Maris Ozols said:

I like very much how your viewer for Lean and TeX code looks like!

Thanks! It is a fun side effect of how the method works that you get all this "natural language glue" between the Lean statements. And there are some nice-looking intermediate nodes for things it formalized along the way:
Expander Mixing Lemma
Hoeffding’s Lemma / One-Step MGF Bound
McDiarmid / Bounded Differences Inequality
Chernoff Tail Bound from MGF
Hypergeometric MGF Comparison
Hypergeometric Counting Tail Bound

It should noted that for all of these intermediate statements the correpsondence between Lean and TeX is only agent verified, the system only promises to deliver on the human-approved semantic meaning of paper targets. Though, in situations like this where nodes were used in a correct proof a substantial theorem that really is faithful to its intended target, it seems to me they are likely to be genuinely useful at a high rate.

Announcing Trellis! Manuscript, code, formalizations are posted.

Manuscript:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09674

Codebase:
https://github.com/wpegden/trellis

Formalizations in pretty viewers linked at:
https://www.math.cmu.edu/~wes/trellis.php

In particular I link to two unconditional formalizations of recent Ramsey theory breakthroughs.

I've put in some work the past few days to simplify the systems side of this so that it will (hopefully) not be too bad for others to get this up and running. Let me know what issues you have and I will try my best to be responsive! All the big three providers are currently supported, though most of my usage is with codex so that's where things are probably best ironed out.
